title: The stamp that found itself
passages:
The Kettering night board ran the length of the west wall, thirty-one screens, eleven rigs posted, four holes where rigs should have been. Kass had the desk terminal open with badge 2241 already in the reader. The channel record keeps the badge of whoever keyed a rig onto the line, and 2241 sat on channel 12-K at 04:51, the minute the fourth ghost rig stopped being anywhere.

They keyed SCRUB.

*KEYED LINES CLOSE FROM THE FAR END.*

"The far end's gone," Kass said.

*FAR END NOT PRESENT. LINE CANNOT CLOSE.*

"Open a discrepancy, then."

*A DISCREPANCY REQUIRES A SECOND KEY.*

They had tried at 02:00 and again at 04:52 and the terminal had said the same three things each time, in the same flat voice, like a man reading a menu he hadn't cooked. Nineteen hours on shift. Their name was going to sit on that channel until the sun went out, and the worst part was that they had keyed it themselves, doing their job, watching a rig delete itself under their own hand.

Boots came in from the yard side at 05:41, unhurried, and stopped at the clock post. Bay 4 coveralls, Shift 2 patch, a face Kass had seen on eleven months of rosters and never once spoken to.

"You're Ospina."

"I'm a loader who'd like to be somewhere else."

"You're Bay 4's seal authority and you walked out of Anza unlogged."

"I walked out of Anza." Ospina put their badge against the post and didn't press. "I'm clocking the oh-six-hundred. Then I'm going home for nine hours and none of this."

"Four rigs came off this board as derelict. Somebody crimped every one of them shut and stamped the plate. There is one seal authority on your shift, and they're standing at my clock post with their hand in their pocket."

Ospina's hand was in their pocket. It stayed there.

"I found that stamp," they said. "In a tool void. I didn't use it. I've now told that to a dispatcher, to a node operator on the open channel, and to you, and it keeps not helping."

"Anza confessed on the open channel an hour ago. Their loader signed the shortfall in front of the whole shop. You heard that from the road, I'd guess."

"I heard it from the road."

"Then you know what a chipped die means when it shows up on a ballast plate." Kass pulled the badge out of the reader and held it, which is not the same as scrubbing it, but it kept the terminal from saying anything else. "A seal authority who misses two boards gets the stamp pulled to the node. You know that. Clock in, keep your die, and then get on a rig with me."

"To Anza." Ospina said it the way you'd say a diagnosis. "Your node's on the record feeding seals down the line. I'm not putting my name inside that."

"Nobody's asking for your name."

"Somebody always is."

Ospina turned to the post, badge up, and Kass had time to think *good, they're going to do it* before the board lit a line nobody had asked for.

*SEAL AUTHORITY LIVE ON FLOOR. BAY FOUR. DIE PRESENT.*

Every clerk in the room looked up. Down at the far end, a man in Bay 4 coveralls stopped walking.

Ospina looked at their own pocket like it had spoken out of turn. "That's not supposed to happen."

"It reads the die, not the badge," Kass said. "You walked a true stamp into a yard that's short one, and you just told every soul on the floor where it is."

The clock over the post said 05:44.

Kass set the badge down on the desk, face up, where they could see it and the terminal couldn't.

"Go home in ten minutes," they said. "I'll walk you to the yard gate myself."

Ospina didn't come off the clock post. "Ten minutes is how long a rig takes to ruin a day."

"It's four records."

They pulled the derelict file. *Derelict* is a line word: a rig that misses two calls isn't lost, isn't stolen, isn't broken. It's derelict, and derelict has a procedure, and the procedure is faster than any of the other three. Kass laid the four side by side on the west wall, one screen each, thirty-one screens and now four of them doing something.

*LK-1180. LK-2266. LK-3071. LK-4519.*

"Read me the wreck report on 1180."

"There isn't one." Ospina came two steps closer, which was two steps more than Kass expected. "No crash line. No scrub line. No tow-in, no shoulder mark, no driver's statement. It just stops answering and then it's on a claim."

Every one of the four had the same three lines under it. A derelict order. A standing reclamation claim. A dispatch.

"Explain the claim to me like I'm a clerk," Kass said, "because I am one."

"A standing claim is an open order that never closes," Ospina said. "Line reclamation keeps a few live forever. Cargo reads as dead weight, an agent gets dispatched, the agent hauls it to a yard and breaks the plate. The discrepancy goes away because the thing making it goes away." They shrugged, unhappy about it. "That's the whole job. Pell's the agent. The fob on his chest is the warrant-token. He can freeze a node's board and its resupply until the node hands over whatever the claim names."

"Four rigs, four claims, one agent."

"Four rigs, four claims." Ospina leaned in and stopped. "Kass. Look at the key line."

Kass looked. Under each claim, the field that records who keyed it: the badge that put the order on the line.

*KEYED: 2241. CHANNEL 12-K.*

"All four."

"I've never keyed a claim," Kass said. "Nineteen months. I key rigs on and rigs off. Claims come down from the line desk with a supervisor's number on them, and I have never once had a supervisor's number."

"Then somebody's wearing yours like a coat." Ospina straightened up. "That's my answer for the four. I can go home."

"There's a fifth."

The fifth claim was open. Not dispatched-and-closed like the others: open, live, pulsing. Destination field, one word. *ANZA.* Target field, a description instead of a number, because there was no number to use.

*UNIT, MEDICAL. NO TRANSPONDER. NOT PRESENT ON ANY BOARD. LAST MASS POSTED: KETTERING NORTH GATE.*

"That's the rig Rhea towed in on a hook," Ospina said. "I was in the yard when it came off the road. Nobody's ever going to find it, it's got no transponder and no plate on the board."

"That's not how it reads from here." Kass tapped the status line. "Anything not on the board reads as derelict. It isn't a judgment, it's a filing status. No board entry, no crew, no cargo, no owner. Free to haul." They scrolled. The dispatch block had a live ETA and a note that the agent was already rolling with his pendant keyed. *AT NODE PRIOR TO 06:00 BOARD.*

Ospina's hand was still in their pocket. It had been in that pocket since 05:41 and Kass was starting to understand it wasn't going to come out for anybody.

"Somebody at Anza confessed on the open channel," Kass said. "Feed the seals down the line, keep the roster fat. And now their ore siding has a rig on it that isn't on any board, and a reclaimer is thirteen minutes out to collect it."

"That's their problem. Their loader signed her own name to it in front of the shop."

Kass scrolled to the bottom of the fifth claim, where the delivery block sits, and turned the screen so Ospina could read it.

*RECEIVED: ANZA. SHIFT ONE. NODE CODE 4-11.*

"Nobody received anything," Ospina said.

"Somebody did," Kass said. "An hour ago. For a rig that isn't on their board."

Ospina didn't answer that. Something behind their face shut and stayed shut.

"Say it," Kass said. "You're the one with the pocket."

"The tool void." Ospina brought the hand out. Empty. They turned it over like that would change anything. "Every rig has one. Gap beside the ballast tray where a crew keeps a crimper, a spare die, a length of chain, so you can reseal a plate out in the yard instead of walking to the shop. I put my arm in one at ten past five, looking for chain. My fingers closed on a die with the corner chipped out of it."

"Which rig."

"LK-4402. Bay Three. Came off the Anza run at 04:20 and hasn't moved since." Ospina looked at the west wall, at the four screens. "I kept telling myself I found it in a bay, like a bay is somewhere else. It's forty meters from your desk."

Kass keyed 4402 onto the second screen from the left. *ON YARD. NO CLAIM. NO ORDER.* A rig with no reason on it to be looked at twice, parked in the same yard the four had gone out of.

"So the man who crimped a loader into a box and stamped ballast on the plate," Kass said, "came back for the day shift and left his tools in Bay Three."

"He never left. He's been walking past me for two days." Ospina's jaw worked. "Two days, and I've had his die in my coat since ten past five."

"And at 05:44 this floor announced a live stamp standing in Bay Four." Kass looked at the clock post. "He heard that. Every soul on the floor heard that."

The out-board is the slate by the yard door, where a loader keys out before the horn and the gate reads the key instead of a badge, because nobody wants to stop a yard at shift change to argue about pockets. Bay Four was already drifting. Coveralls, Shift Two patch, a chain bag over one shoulder, no hurry anywhere in him. He crossed to the slate, keyed, and kept walking.

Then he turned his head toward the west wall.

"Is that him?"

"That's the man who stamped the plates," Ospina said, and their arm came up halfway.

The horn went. It lives in the roof over the clock post and it is built to be heard over a running yard, and for three full seconds it took Ospina's voice, and Ospina's half-raised hand, and everything else in the room. The man's eyes went to Ospina's pocket through the glass. He didn't stop and he didn't hurry. Out the yard door, left, and Bay Three is the second door on the left.

Ospina's arm came down. "He knows what I'm carrying."

"He knows the die is out of the box," Kass said. "That's worse for him than knowing who's holding it."

"He'll strip that void down to the tray plate. There'll be nothing in Bay Three to find by the time anybody looks."

Kass turned to the out-board to log the hour, and stopped with their hand on the keys.

*SIGNED OUT 05:47. NO BADGE PRESENTED.*

"That's not a thing the board lets you do," Kass said.

"No," Ospina said. "It isn't."

The sign-out sat on the west wall in amber with a flag beside it, and a flag at Kettering means a clerk with a supervisor's number has to come and stand in front of it, and at 05:48 there are no clerks.

"Bay Three," Ospina said. "There's a floor buffer at 06:20. It walks the bays with a magnet and a scraper. Whatever's in that void is in a bin by 06:25."

"Then we don't go and look in Bay Three." Kass sat and pulled the standing-order index. "He can't invent his own procedure. A reclaimer works off a number the line desk keeps live forever. Nine of those. Nobody reads them because they never close."

"I've read two."

"Then read this one over my shoulder." Kass keyed it up. *RL-0900 SERIES. RECLAMATION OF DEAD WEIGHT.*

*A CLAIM CLOSES ON DEAD WEIGHT ONLY.*

*CARGO ENTERED ON A NODE BOARD AS CREW, AND COUNTERSIGNED BY A LIVE SEAL AUTHORITY, IS NOT WEIGHT. THE AGENT SHALL CARRY IT AS CREW AND DELIVER IT TO THE LINE DESK AS A LIVING WITNESS.*

*A COUNTERSIGN STRUCK WITH A FALSE DIE, OR WITH A DIE NOT PRESENT IN THE SIGNING HAND, IS VOID. THE CARGO REVERTS TO WEIGHT.*

Ospina read it twice. "Say the middle part out loud. I want to hear it in the room."

"He can't close the claim," Kass said. "Not on a man who's on a board as crew with a live die under him. The order stops being a haul and turns into a delivery, and he'd have to walk him into a desk breathing, where somebody writes down what he says." They tapped the screen. "That rig of his has a cradle on the back and a hook on the arm. There's no bench on it. He carries four hundred twelve kilos or he carries nothing."

"And the last part is the trick."

"The last part is why he's in a hurry. The board compares the strike to the register. Every die leaves a corner pattern, and a recut die leaves a clean one. A photograph of a die isn't a die. It has to be steel, in a hand, at the plate." Kass opened the die register for the district. "Three inside five hundred klicks."

*4-11-ANN. HOLDER: ANZA, BAY FOUR. STATUS: IMPOUNDED. DISCREPANCY OPEN.*

"That one signed a shortfall in front of its own shop an hour ago," Ospina said. "It's in a bag with a tag on it. A die under a discrepancy can't strike anything, it's dead paper."

*9-02. HOLDER: LINE DESK EAST. 540 Klicks. STATUS: COURIER BOX, SEALED. BREAK REQUIRES TWO SUPERVISORS.*

"Out of range, out of road, and out of time."

"Then there's mine," Ospina said, "and mine's not on there, because I never reported it, because I found it."

"It's on here." Kass turned the screen. *KETTERING, BAY FOUR. ISSUED: 4-11-K. REPORTED: NOTHING. NEVER REPORTED.* Below that, the field that records the last plate the die touched.

*LAST GOOD IMPRESSION: BALLAST PLATE, MEDICAL UNIT. KETTERING NORTH GATE. PRIOR NIGHT. 412 KG.*

"An hour ago a node operator at Anza read that plate out on the open channel," Kass said. "Line by line, in front of his whole shop. Bay Four. Shift Two. Four hundred twelve kilos. Ballast. And then a man walked in and asked what ballast meant."

Ospina said nothing at all, which was new.

"The die that wrote him down as weight has been in your coat since ten past five," Kass said. "It's the only true one inside five hundred klicks. It's not a coincidence you're holding it. It's the whole door."

"There's another field under that," Ospina said.

There was. Kass read it out because reading things out is the job.

*COUNTERSIGN BINDS THE HOLDER OF THE DIE TO THE CONSIGNMENT.*

Ospina's hand went back in their pocket.

Down the yard, past the glass, the Bay Three door stood open with the light on, and the clock over the post said 05:50.

The field sat on the screen without blinking. *COUNTERSIGN BINDS THE HOLDER OF THE DIE TO THE CONSIGNMENT.*

Ospina's fingers closed around the chipped steel in their pocket. The corner pattern was still there, worn but readable — the same pattern the board would check against the register when the strike came down. If it came down.

"I'm not putting my name on a consignment I didn't make," Ospina said. "I found a die in a void. I didn't crimp a plate. I didn't stamp ballast on a man's coffin. Signing that field says I did."

"Signing that field says you're the authority who countersigns a living witness," Kass said. "The consignment already exists. Anza confessed to it on open channel. Nour's signature, your shift's shortfall, four hundred twelve kilos logged as ballast. The only question is whether the weight gets a name before Pell hauls it off."

"And if the die's false?"

"Then the cargo reverts to weight and Pell wins. But this die isn't false. It's the one that wrote the first entry. The board will read the corner pattern and it will match." Kass tapped the screen where the register showed the last good impression. *BALLAST PLATE, MEDICAL UNIT. KETTERING NORTH GATE. PRIOR NIGHT. 412 KG.* "You're not admitting you stood at the box. You're admitting the tool that put him in is the only tool that can write him out."

Ospina didn't move. The clock over the post ticked to 05:51.

"Bay Three door's still open," they said. "He's in there right now stripping the void. By the time a floor buffer hits it, there's nothing to find. No chain, no crimper, no second die. He walked past the board when it announced me. He knows the stamp's live. He knows what that means for his claim."

"Then he knows he has to move faster than we do." Kass stood, rolling their shoulders. "Which rig runs fastest to Anza."

Ospina's hand came out of the pocket. The chipped die sat on their palm, dull gray in the board light, one corner bitten clean off like a chipped tooth.

"Service rig 7-K," they said. "North yard, bay six. It's a line rig, not a hauler — no cradle, no hook, just an engine and a cab and a dish that talks to the desk. Does 140 on the haul road if the tires hold. I've run it twice on courier runs." They closed their fingers back around the steel. "But it's a line rig. That means a dispatcher has to key it out. And the only dispatcher on this floor is sitting at a desk with badge 2241 face up on the reader, and the board still thinks they keyed four reclamation claims they never touched."

Kass looked at their own badge on the desk. The number stared back.

"I can key it," they said. "But the rig logs the keying badge. 2241 on a line rig heading for Anza with a seal authority who never reported their die — that's a flag the line desk will see before we clear the node."

"Then don't key it as 2241."

"There's no other badge on this floor."

Ospina tilted their head toward the clock post. "There's a badge on the out-board. Signed out 05:47, no badge presented. The forger's key. He used a ghost number to walk out. The board doesn't know whose ghost."

"A ghost key on a line rig with a live stamp and a reclaimer thirteen minutes out from Anza." Kass picked up their badge, turned it over in their hand. "The line desk will scrub that rig off the road before we hit the county line."

"Not if the rig's already moving when they see it." Ospina pocketed the die. "Key it. I'll be at bay six. If the desk scrubs us, we're moving. They can't stop a rig that's already on the road from the far end — they need a near-end key to cut power, and the near end is us."

"And if Pell's got a near-end key on his cradle?"

"Then we're dead either way. But we're not dead at Anza." Ospina started for the yard door, then stopped. "The standing order. RL-0900. Read me the delivery block again."

Kass pulled it up. *DELIVERY: LINE DESK. LIVING WITNESS. COUNTERSIGN REQUIRED. AGENT SHALL NOT RELEASE CARGO WITHOUT COUNTERSIGN VERIFIED.*

"The agent shall not release," Kass read. "Pell has to deliver him to a desk. He can't just dump the pod."

"He can't dump the pod," Ospina agreed. "But he can sit on the node's board and its resupply until the desk takes the witness. And the desk won't take a witness without a countersign. And the only countersign that holds is the one in my pocket." They looked at Kass. "Which means I don't just have to get to Anza. I have to get to Anza, find the node board, strike the plate, and hand the witness over — before Pell decides the discrepancy's closed enough to walk away from."

The clock said 05:53.

"Bay six," Ospina said. "North yard. Don't wait for me to climb in."

They were gone through the door before Kass could answer.

Kass sat down at the terminal, badge 2241 in hand, and keyed the service rig onto the line.

*UNIT 7-K. KEYED: 2241. CHANNEL 12-K. STATUS: DISPATCHED.*

The board didn't flag it. The board didn't scrub it. The board just accepted the line like it had accepted the four claims, like it accepted everything that came through badge 2241 on channel 12-K.

Kass stood, grabbed their coat from the back of the chair, and ran for the north yard.

Behind them, the west wall shed another ghost number. *LK-4402. CLAIM FILED. DISPATCH PENDING.*

The forger had moved fast.
